notes:
Below are notes on 2 Corinthians 3, verse by verse. Every point comes from a page I actually read or saw in search results, with its URL. Where I found nothing, I left it out; the list of gaps is at the end.

---

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Utley says both questions are worded to expect the answer "no." Paul uses this term often in 2 Corinthians because of the conflict with the aggressive false teachers from Palestine ("as some"). He adds that the early church used letters of recommendation to assure the orthodoxy and trustworthiness of itinerant ministers. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3
- Henrietta Mears (quoted on Precept Austin) says Paul's main troublemakers were Jewish law teachers who carried letters of introduction. She asks why Paul would need a letter to a church he founded himself. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-3-commentary

**v. 2**
- Utley: Paul needs no letter because he founded the church. "Written in our hearts" (perfect passive) means they stayed permanently in his heart, and the passive points to God as the source of that love. "By all men" is overstatement. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3
- Mears applies it: the world rarely studies God's Word but does study God's people, so a Christian's life is an open letter. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-3-commentary

**v. 3**
- Guzik: The Corinthian Christians were indeed Paul's letter of recommendation, yet he realized that he did not write that letter – Jesus did. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Utley reads "tablets of stone… human hearts" as a contrast between the old covenant as an outside law and the new covenant as an inner one (Jer 31; Ezek 36). — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3
- Precept Austin, on the word *plax* (tablet): under the new covenant the Spirit writes the Law inside the believer instead of on stone. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-3-commentary
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that the Sinai tablets were not written with ink, but "graven" by "the finger of God". Christ's letter is better still, being written by the Spirit of the living God. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Cr/2Cr_003.cfm
- Geneva notes: Paul sets God's power against ordinary ink to show the work was God's. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html

**v. 4**
- Utley: "confidence" comes from the same Greek root as faith and trust, and means reliance. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3
- Geneva: this is the boldness Paul shows about the worth and fruit of his ministry. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html

**v. 5**
- Matthew Henry: on our own we cannot even think a good thought. This is true concerning ministers and all Christians; the best are no more than what the grace of God makes them. — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Cr/2Cr_003.cfm
- Ligonier quotes Augustine: "Our sufficiency is from God, in whose power are our heart and our thoughts." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-death-dealing-letter
- Guzik: only Jesus is equal to the task of changing lives. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/

**v. 6**
- Ellicott (Biblehub): "letter" here does not mean the literal sense of Scripture as opposed to an allegorical one. It stands, not for what we call the literal meaning of Scripture, as contrasted with one which is allegorical or spiritual, but for the whole written code or law of Judaism. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/3-6.htm
- Guzik agrees: Paul is not ranking experience above the word, or allegory above literal reading. He is showing that the new covenant is better. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Utley also says the passage does not set out a method of interpretation. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3
- Pulpit Commentary: the Law, taken as an outward letter, sentences to death those who disobey it, and no one obeys it perfectly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/3-6.htm
- Gill: the law kills by provoking sin, by convicting the sinner, and by threatening and inflicting death. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/3-6.html
- Barnes: the Law produced guilt and condemnation, not pardon or joy. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/3-6.html
- Matthew Henry widens the warning: if we rest only in the letter of the gospel we shall be never the better for so doing. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/3-6.html

**v. 7**
- Geneva: the words "engraved in stones" show Paul speaks not of the ceremonies of the Law, but of the ten commandments. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html
- Barnes: the "glory" was God's appearing on Sinai, with thunder and fire. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/3-7.htm
- Gill: the law is a "ministration of death" because it set bodily death as the penalty for each commandment, and it also carries eternal death. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/3-7.htm
- Vincent (quoted on Precept Austin): the phrase refers to Moses' particular role at Sinai, not his whole career. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_37-11_commentary
- Guzik: calling it a "ministry of death" is fair, because that is what the law does to us: It slays us as guilty sinners before God so that we can be resurrected by the new covenant. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/

**v. 8**
- Geneva: in the new covenant God gives the Spirit not as a dead thing, but a living Spirit, working life. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html
- Guzik: if a covenant that brought death had glory, expect more glory from the one that brings the Spirit and life. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/

**v. 9**
- Ligonier: The old covenant delivers the verdict of "unrighteous" to sinners, for we have not perfectly kept its demands, but the new covenant delivers the verdict of "righteous" to sinners who trust in Jesus. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-glory-of-the-new-covenant
- Geneva: "righteousness" means Christ. Because he is credited to us, we are not condemned and are even crowned as righteous. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik: the new covenant outshines the old just as the sun always outshines the brightest moon. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Ligonier compares John 1:17. John does not deny there was grace under the old covenant; it is simply seen far more clearly in Christ. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/the-glory-of-the-new-covenant
- Biblehub Q&A: "no glory now" does not deny the law's value. The old covenant has been surpassed, and the law still shows sin and points to the Savior. — https://biblehub.com/q/how_does_2_cor_3_10_reconcile_with_ot_law.htm
- MacArthur: we're not waiting for a new new covenant. — https://gty.org/library/sermons-library/47-18

**v. 11**
- Pulpit Commentary notes that Paul changes his wording. The passing covenant came "through glory," it was a transitory gleam; the abiding covenant is "in glory;" i.e. an eternal splendour. — https://biblehub.com/2_corinthians/3-11.htm
- Utley: the contrast is not between what is from God and what is not. It is between a lesser glory and a greater, lasting one. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3

**v. 12**
- Guzik: The old covenant restricted and separated men from God; the new covenant brings us to God and enables us to come *boldly* to Him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Vincent: the bold, open speech answers the opponents' charge that Paul was hiding something. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_312-14_commentary
- Geneva: the gospel states plainly what the Law showed only dimly. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html

**v. 13** (what the veil was for is debated)
- Guzik: the veil hid the *fading* of the glory, not the shining itself. So the contrast is both passing versus lasting and hidden versus revealed. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Bernard (on Precept Austin) notes that the KJV takes "end" (*telos*) to mean Christ, the fulfilment of the law. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_312-14_commentary
- Swindoll (same page): the veil shows that, away from God's presence, our sinful weakness cannot keep hold of God's glory. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_312-14_commentary
- Geneva: the veil was a sign of the darkness and weakness in people, who were dulled by the Law's brightness. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html

**v. 14**
- P. E. Hughes: Israel would not receive what God was saying through Moses, so their understanding became dull and deadened. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_312-14_commentary
- Guzik: because the veil stays on, they cannot see that Moses' glory has faded and that they should now look to Jesus. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: since the same veil now lies on their heart, they still think there is something superior or more glorious in the ministry of Moses. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/

**v. 16**
- Guzik: only a work of God, turning a person to the Lord, takes the veil away. Turning to the Lord is also how anyone gets the "unveiled face" of v. 18. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Geneva: Christ's coming removes the covering and turns hearts to the Lord. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html

**v. 17**
- Guzik: Moses was free to remove the veil when he was with the Lord. We have the Holy Spirit, who is the Lord, so we share that freedom. He takes "liberty" mainly as the *liberty of access*. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Precept Austin: the Spirit moves a person from legalistic bondage into liberty, including liberty from the curse of sin. — https://temp.preceptaustin.org/2-corinthians-3-commentary

**v. 18**
- Precept Austin: the verb is present tense (an ongoing process) and passive (the Spirit does the work). We cannot transform ourselves any more than we could save (justify) ourselves. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_318_commentary
- The same page: the mirror is the gospel, and William MacDonald says what only Moses had is now every believer's privilege. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_318_commentary
- Guzik: "beholding" means careful study, not a casual look. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Ligonier: the verse describes our sanctification and finally our glorification. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/from-glory-to-glory

---

## Where Protestant traditions differ

**v. 6–7: How does the law "kill," and which law is meant?**
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** the chapter is a law/gospel text. The law cannot accomplish in us what it demands of us. Preaching the law, however sincerely, cannot give life or lift the veil; only the gospel gives righteousness. — https://www.1517.org/articles/law-and-gospel-in-2-corinthians-3
- **Reformed (Calvin):** the law is called "letter" because it is "dead preaching" in itself. Its role is to show the disease without offering a cure. — https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol40/htm/ix.ii.htm
  - An editor's note on the same page qualifies this: the law kills not by its own nature but because of human corruption, when it is treated as a covenant of works. — https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol40/htm/ix.ii.htm
  - Geneva notes go further: if Moses' ministry is taken by itself, even the Ten Commandments are "abolished." — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html
- **Baptist (MacArthur):** the Ten Commandments are meant, and the law does is kill. Yet the law is now written on our hearts, and the indwelling Spirit enables us to fulfil it. — https://www.gty.org/sermons/47-17/the-glory-of-the-new-covenant-part-3
- **Gill (Baptist):** the law's killing effect comes from human corruption, not from the law's design, so the law itself is not to blame. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-corinthians/3-6.html
- **Utley (evangelical):** Christians are not under Old Testament law. This is not because it has passed away but because believers fulfil it through love, and it remains God's will for human society. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3
- **Anglican voices (Biblehub sermons):** Canon Scott-Holland says the letter is the moral law and that it killed "by God's own intention" in order to convict. Another sermon on the same page broadens the idea: any letter kills when people stop at it and never reach the spirit. — https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_corinthians/3-6.htm

**v. 17: Who is "the Lord"?**
- Geneva (Reformed): Christ is that Spirit who takes away that covering. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel / charismatic-friendly): the Holy Spirit is the Lord. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Precept Austin: the Spirit holds the place in the new covenant that the Lord held in the old. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_37-11_commentary
- Utley lists the "Lord of Exodus" as the Spirit of Jesus. He calls Paul's use of "spirit" in vv. 6, 8, 17 and 18 "highly ambiguous": it is unclear whether Paul means the Holy Spirit or "the spiritual," and Utley thinks the overlap may be deliberate. — https://bible.org/seriespage/2-corinthians-3

**v. 17: Charismatic "liberty"**
- Guzik, though friendly to charismatic teaching, warns that the verse does not license any Pentecostal or Charismatic excess. There is no liberty to disobey what the Spirit says in Scripture. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/

**v. 18: Who is "we all," and is the change step by step?**
- Geneva holds that Paul is speaking properly of the ministers of the Gospel, judging by what comes before and after. — https://www.ccel.org/g/geneva/notes/2Corinthians/3.html
- Guzik says it belongs to all believers, not a privileged few. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-corinthians-3/
- Ellicott (Anglican): "glory to glory" means less that of passing from one stage of glory to another than the idea that this transfiguring process, which begins with glory, will find its consummation also in glory. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_corinthians/3-18.htm
- Piper (Baptist) notes the same grammatical possibility (beginning and goal, not gradual steps). — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/see-glory-be-glorious
- Precept Austin, by contrast, stresses a gradual, lifelong process ending in bodily change when Christ appears. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2corinthians_318_commentary

---

## Other views

**Orthodox (v. 18, with v. 13):**
- Fr. Vladimir Berzonsky (OCA): Christ's glory makes believers "ever-brighter icons" of his image. Those who are baptized, sealed with the Spirit and keep their hearts open move from one stage of glory to the next. We are invited to become like God in every way except sharing the divine essence, and can keep growing even after this life. He also calls this an active struggle against the passions. — https://www.oca.org/reflections/berzonsky/from-glory-to-glory
- An Enduring Word article notes that Eastern Orthodoxy puts its emphasis on this transformation, called *theosis*. It warns that at times the idea was taken too far and it was thought Man could attain an almost god-like state. — https://post.enduringword.com/from-to-what-it-means-to-be-saved/

---

**What I couldn't find:**
- Catholic commentary (newadvent, catholic.com): only the Douay-Rheims wording.
- Methodist/Wesleyan notes (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed).
- Pentecostal sources beyond Guzik (ag.org, pneumareview, samstorms).
- NET Bible notes and bibleodyssey.org.
- Anything on how hyper-grace, prosperity or word-of-faith teachers use this chapter.

These could fill out v. 6 (letter and spirit in older Catholic reading), v. 17 and the debated popular teaching.
